这与 OpenAPI 有着根本的不同。OpenAPI 规范是为开发者工具设计的静态文档。而 MCP 的 tools/list 是一种实时的协议交互：代理提问，服务器回答，然后代理进行适应调整。
一个协议，适用于所有服务器
这就是标准化在实践中如此重要的原因：每个 MCP 服务器，无论它连接什么服务或数据，都使用相同的协议并遵循相同的模式。工具调用流程始终是 tools/call。发现流程始终是 tools/list。初始化握手也始终相同。
如果 AI 代理想要与五个不同的服务（GitHub、Slack、数据库、Google 日历和文件系统）进行交互，并且每个服务都有一个 MCP 服务器，那么代理将对这五个服务使用完全相同的协议。无需自定义适配器，也无需特定于服务的集成代码。一次构建，多处集成。
有状态会话
MCP 在客户端和服务器之间维持一个持久会话。在初始化期间，双方会通告各自支持的内容。服务器声明它是否提供工具、资源或订阅，而客户端声明它能处理什么。这种相互握手为会话创建了一份契约。
在该会话中，上下文得以保留。当 AI 代理打开文件、运行测试并识别错误时，它不会在步骤之间丢失上下文。这与 REST 的无状态模型恰恰相反，对于每个操作都依赖于之前发生的多步骤代理工作流来说，这一点至关重要。
REST 与 MCP 概览
MCP 与 REST：是分层，而非对立
这是在“MCP 对比 REST”的框架中被忽略的部分：在大多数实际实现中，MCP 服务器在内部使用 REST API 来完成其实际工作。
以 GitHub MCP 服务器为一个具体例子。它将 repository/list 等高级 MCP 工具作为原语暴露出来，任何 AI 代理都可以通过标准 MCP 协议发现并调用这些原语。但在内部，它将每次工具调用转换为相应的 GitHub REST API 请求。MCP 层负责发现、会话管理，并提供统一接口。REST API 则负责实际的 GitHub 操作。
这种模式在整个生态系统中不断重复。无论是 Stripe、Slack、Notion 还是 Salesforce，MCP 服务器通常是一个轻量级的智能层，在 MCP 协议与底层服务的原生 REST API 之间进行转换。
MCP 和 REST 并非竞争性技术。它们是 AI 技术栈中互补的层。MCP 在 REST API 已经提供的底层功能之上，提供了一个对 AI 友好的接口。如今，你可以找到用于文件系统、Google Maps、Docker、Spotify、Stripe 以及越来越多企业服务的 MCP 服务器，而在底层，它们几乎都在调用 REST API。
为结果设计，而非为端点设计
开发者在采用 MCP 时最常犯的错误是自动将每个 REST 端点转换为 MCP 工具。像 FastMCP 的 OpenAPI 转换器这样的工具让这种做法变得很诱人：只需一行代码，你的整个 API 就暴露给了 LLM。
问题在于，优秀的 REST API 和优秀的 MCP 服务器有着根本不同的设计目标。
REST API 是慷慨的。它提供数百个小型、可组合的端点，因为程序化迭代的成本很低。人类开发者只需阅读一次文档，他们的代码就可以通过快速的网络跳转将 get_user()、get_orders(user_id) 和 get_order_details(order_id) 串联起来。对于开发者来说，选择越多越好。
当你把同样的接口交给 LLM 代理时，你不是在赋予它能力，而是在淹没它。代理必须将每个工具描述加载到其上下文窗口中，为每一个描述支付 token 成本，并推理出你的五十个与用户相关的工具中该调用哪一个。代理迭代在程序化迭代所没有的方面是昂贵的：每次交互中，每一个额外的工具都会消耗 token 并增加延迟。
更好的方法是：围绕用户想要实现的目标来设计 MCP 工具，而不是围绕你的内部 API 结构。
糟糕的做法：三个独立的工具：get_user、get_orders、get_shipments；要求代理进行三次往返，并在对话历史中保存中间结果。
好的做法：一个工具（track_order(email)），在内部调用所有三个端点，并返回一个完整的、结合上下文的答案，例如“订单 #12345 已通过 FedEx 发货，将于周四送达。”
相同的结果，一次调用，为实际消费者而设计。把你的 MCP 服务器看作一个用户界面：就像你应用于 UI 的产品思维一样，只不过是为了非人类用户。
身份验证：MCP 的强约定方案
REST API 支持多种身份验证机制：API 密钥、Basic 认证、Bearer 令牌、OAuth 2.0、自定义标头、双向 TLS。这种灵活性既是优势（适合任何用例），也是劣势（每次集成都需要自己的身份验证实现）。
MCP 采取了强约定的立场：带 PKCE 的 OAuth 2.1 是标准。MCP 授权规范经历了多次修订（2025 年 3 月、2025 年 6 月、2025 年 11 月），定义了客户端如何发现授权要求、动态注册以及获取限定范围的访问令牌。
这对企业级部署至关重要。当 AI 代理代表用户执行操作时，你需要知道是哪个用户授权了哪些操作。OAuth 2.1 的作用域令牌（scoped tokens）解决了这个问题：每个访问令牌都明确声明了它授权访问的资源和操作，MCP 服务器可以在调用工具时验证该令牌是否具有该操作所需的特定作用域。
WorkOS AuthKit 支持 OAuth 2.1，可作为 MCP 应用程序的兼容授权服务器。它处理了不断演进的协议的复杂性（动态客户端注册、客户端 ID 元数据文档 (CIMD)、令牌验证、受保护资源元数据），让开发者可以专注于构建实际工具，而不是从头开始实现 OAuth 提供程序。
何时使用哪种方案
在以下情况保留你的 REST API：
Web 和移动应用程序，其中客户端是开发者编写的代码，确切知道要调用什么。
高吞吐量数据获取，其中 HTTP 缓存、CDN 和负载均衡器能提供性能优势。
第三方开发者集成，由人类开发者使用 SDK 和文档来调用你的 API。
微服务通信，服务之间以明确定义的模式相互调用。
在以下情况添加 MCP：
AI 代理是你的消费者。如果你正在为 Claude、ChatGPT、Cursor 或任何由 LLM 驱动的工具进行构建，MCP 为它们提供了一种无需定制集成代码即可发现和使用你的 API 的方法。
你需要多步骤工作流。有状态会话意味着代理可以将操作串联起来而不会丢失上下文。
你希望实现一次编写即可集成的效果。构建一个 MCP 服务器，它就能与任何兼容 MCP 的客户端配合使用；无需为每个模型编写自定义适配器。
你需要对代理访问进行细粒度授权。带有作用域令牌的 OAuth 2.1 为你提供了企业所需的控制能力。
实用架构
在大多数生产环境中，MCP 并不会取代你的 REST API，而是对其进行封装：

┌──────────────────────────────────┐
│  LLM Agent (Claude, Cursor...)   │
│  ↕ JSON-RPC / MCP Protocol       │
├──────────────────────────────────┤
│  MCP Server                      │
│  - Tool discovery & catalog      │
│  - Stateful session management   │
│  - Auth (OAuth 2.1)              │
│  - Outcome-oriented tool logic   │
│  ↕ HTTP                          │
├──────────────────────────────────┤
│  Your REST API                   │
│  - Business logic                │
│  - Data access                   │
│  - Existing infrastructure       │
└──────────────────────────────────┘
你的 REST API 继续不变地为你的 Web 应用、移动应用和第三方集成提供服务。你的 MCP 服务器作为新的接口层与其并行存在，提供代理所需的 AI 原生协议。
入门指南
如果你已经有一个带有 OpenAPI 规范的 REST API，最快的途径是使用该规范作为起点，但要克制自动转换所有内容的冲动。相反，你应该：
确定你的用户会要求 AI 代理使用你的 API 执行的前五个工作流。
为这些工作流设计面向结果的工具。每个工具都应能在一次调用中返回完整且有用的结果。
将你的 REST API 用作后端。你的 MCP 服务器在内部调用你现有的端点，无需重写业务逻辑。
实现 OAuth 2.1 进行身份验证。使用像 WorkOS AuthKit 这样开箱即支持 MCP 授权要求的身份提供商。
使用真实的 MCP 客户端进行测试。连接到 Claude Desktop、Cursor 或 MCP Inspector，以验证代理的体验是否合适。
这些 SDK 已经足够成熟，可用于生产环境。FastMCP (Python)、官方 MCP TypeScript SDK 以及像 Stainless 这样的平台可以加速服务器的创建。但最重要的工作不在于工具，而在于设计。平庸的 MCP 服务器与优秀的 MCP 服务器之间的区别，就像糟糕的 UI 与优秀的 UI 之间的区别一样：在于理解你的用户。只不过这个用户恰好是一个 LLM。
总结
REST API 并不会消失。对于传统软件客户端、高性能数据访问以及面向开发者的集成而言，它们仍然是正确的选择。但是，当客户端是一个 LLM agent 时——它需要在运行时发现功能、推理该使用哪个工具，并在多步骤任务中保持上下文——单靠 REST 就不够了。
MCP 提供了缺失的这一层：运行时发现、有状态会话、标准化身份验证，以及一个从零开始为 AI agent 实际工作方式而设计的协议。两者并非竞争性标准，而是技术栈中互补的层：
你的 REST API 负责处理业务逻辑。
MCP 让 AI agent 能够访问这些逻辑，而 AI agent 正日益成为用户与软件交互的主要方式。
为这一未来进行构建的企业，将在 agent 成为默认交互界面时做好充分准备。

blocks.text: 4th August 2026

I released LLM 0.32 this morning, the most significant new version of LLM since the initial launch of the project. The new version includes support for visible reasoning traces, server-side provider tools, redesigned content-addressable SQLite logs, new models, and new features enabled by the OpenAI Responses API. I also released a new version of the llm-anthropic plugin with substantial updates of its own.
Headline features for LLM CLI users

Running LLM against reasoning models now displays their reasoning traces to standard error, so you can see what they are “thinking” without that information being included in the standard output that you might pipe to another tool. Add -R/--hide-reasoning to turn this off.
LLM includes support out-of-the-box for the GPT-5.6 model family, and the new default model used with llm "prompt" is now the inexpensive but capable GPT-5.6 Luna.
LLM calls can now use server-side tools from various providers. OpenAI provide a code execution environment as a server-side tool; LLM can now run prompts that benefit from that like so:
llm --tool CodeInterpreter 'Show current python and SQLite versions'
OpenAI also gets a WebSearch tool.
The llm-anthropic plugin adds WebSearch, WebFetch, CodeExecution, and AnthropicMCP, which looks like this:

llm -m claude-sonnet-5 -T 'AnthropicMCP("https://datasette.simonwillison.net/-/mcp")' \
  'how many rows in the blog_blogmark table?'
That causes Anthropic to execute MCP calls against my new datasette-mcp plugin as part of a single request/response interaction with their API.

The new llm openai endpoint command provides a tool for executing prompts against any OpenAI compatible endpoint as a one-liner. These aren’t logged, which makes this a handy tool for running one-off prompts against anything that speaks the lingua franca of the LLM API world.

Here’s how I use that to run prompts against Gemma 4 12B running in my localhost LM Studio API, via uvx (no LLM installation required) and mixing in the llm-tools-quickjs tool plugin for good measure:

uvx --with llm-tools-quickjs \
  llm openai endpoint http://localhost:1234/v1 -m google/gemma-4-12b \
  -T QuickJS 'Use QuickJS to multiply 3434 * 2434' --td
New features in the Python API

LLM’s Python API previously required you to create a conversation and then send messages to it one at a time. This was an abstraction over the true nature of LLMs, where each request carries a complete history of the messages that came before it. That abstraction started to get in the way for some more advanced cases, so the new release introduces a model.prompt(messages=[]) parameter that can be used like this:

import llm
from llm import user, assistant, system

model = llm.get_model("gpt-5.6-luna")

response = model.prompt(messages=[
    system("You are a helpful pirate."),
    user("What is the capital of France?"),
    assistant("Paris, matey."),
    user("And Germany?"),
])
print(response.text())

LLM previously returned an iterable sequence of strings from each prompt. This worked great when models returned a string response, but failed to predict the weird shape that models would evolve towards. Today many models return a mix of reasoning text, output strings, tool calls, and even image attachments. With LLM 0.32 you can do this instead:
Combine these features and we can finally provide a robust implementation of the semi-standard OpenAI chat completions API, which I’ve now released as the llm-chat-completions-server plugin:

llm install llm-chat-completions-server
llm chat-completions-server --port 9000
# Server is now running on http://127.0.0.1:9000/v1
Now you can run prompts against LLM via that server, using the new llm openai endpoint command!
llm openai endpoint http://127.0.0.1:9000/v1 'hello' -m gpt-5.4-mini

The bigger challenge with that kind of API concerns logging. If we’re going to support the pattern where the message sequence is appended to on every request, ideally we can avoid logging all of that duplicate JSON for every turn.

The solution is the new content-addressable message store, modeled after Git. You can see the new schema for that in the documentation, but the llm logs and llm logs --json commands have both been upgraded to convert that format back into something that’s easy to consume.
And the rest
There is a whole lot more in this release. The 0.32 release notes are pretty comprehensive, and the notes for 0.32rc2, 0.32rc, 0.32a3, 0.32a2, and 0.32a0 should fill in any gaps.

Existing LLM plugins should all continue to work, but plugins that provide extra models will need to be upgraded to 0.32 in order to participate fully in the new streaming events system. There’s a guide to implementing plugins with Structured messages and streaming events in the documentation.
I’ve updated some of my own plugins:
llm-anthropic 0.26 adds support for the Claude 5 family of models, plus WebSearch, WebFetch, CodeExecution, and AnthropicMCP server-side tools.
llm-gemini and llm-openrouter and llm-mistral are nearly there, releases coming soon.
I guess LLM is an agent framework now

Quite a few of the lower-level tools changes in this release were driven by the needs of Datasette Agent. When I started work on LLM, the term “agent” had such a vague definition that I refused to use it. In September 2025 I came around to the idea that "An LLM agent runs tools in a loop to achieve a goal" is well established enough now that I could stop avoiding the term entirely.
Tool chains can now pause for human approval and resume from a stored message history—both needed by Datasette Agent.

Looking at LLM today it’s beginning to look very agent-shaped to me. There’s something neat about having a CLI utility that can mix and match different tools from different sources with different models all as a one-liner, and that includes a Python library powerful enough to build systems like Datasette Agent and llm-coding-agent.
Maybe the next version of LLM will bake the concept of an “agent” into the core library. I’m still trying to figure out what that would look like.

translations: 今天早上我发布了 LLM 0.32，这是该项目自最初发布以来最重要的全新版本。新版本支持可见的推理轨迹、服务端提供商工具、重新设计的内容寻址 SQLite 日志、新模型以及由 OpenAI Responses API 启用的新功能。我还发布了 llm-anthropic 插件的新版本，该版本本身也有大量更新。
LLM CLI 用户的主要功能
现在使用 LLM 运行推理模型时，会将它们的推理轨迹显示到标准错误输出中，这样你就可以看到它们在“思考”什么，而不会将这些信息包含在可能通过管道传递给另一个工具的标准输出中。添加 -R/--hide-reasoning 可以关闭此功能。
LLM 开箱即支持 GPT-5.6 模型系列，并且与 llm "prompt" 一起使用的新默认模型现在是价格低廉但功能强大的 GPT-5.6 Luna。
LLM 调用现在可以使用来自各种提供商的服务端工具。OpenAI 提供了一个代码执行环境作为服务端工具；LLM 现在可以运行从中受益的提示词，如下所示：
llm --tool CodeInterpreter 'Show current python and SQLite versions'
OpenAI 还获得了一个 WebSearch 工具。
llm-anthropic 插件添加了 WebSearch、WebFetch、CodeExecution 和 AnthropicMCP，如下所示：

llm -m claude-sonnet-5 -T 'AnthropicMCP("https://datasette.simonwillison.net/-/mcp")' \
  'how many rows in the blog_blogmark table?'
这使得 Anthropic 在与其 API 进行单次请求/响应交互的过程中，针对我的新 datasette-mcp 插件执行 MCP 调用。
新的 llm openai endpoint 命令提供了一个工具，可以通过单行命令对任何兼容 OpenAI 的端点执行提示词。这些操作不会被记录，这使得它成为一个非常方便的工具，可用于对任何使用 LLM API 世界通用语言的对象运行一次性提示词。
以下是我如何通过 uvx（无需安装 LLM）使用它来对运行在本地主机 LM Studio API 中的 Gemma 4 12B 运行提示词，并顺便混入 llm-tools-quickjs 工具插件：

uvx --with llm-tools-quickjs \
  llm openai endpoint http://localhost:1234/v1 -m google/gemma-4-12b \
  -T QuickJS 'Use QuickJS to multiply 3434 * 2434' --td
Python API 中的新功能
LLM 的 Python API 以前要求你创建一个对话，然后一次向其发送一条消息。这是对 LLM 真实本质的一种抽象，即每个请求都携带之前消息的完整历史记录。这种抽象在一些更高级的用例中开始成为障碍，因此新版本引入了一个 model.prompt(messages=[]) 参数，可以像这样使用：

import llm
from llm import user, assistant, system

model = llm.get_model("gpt-5.6-luna")

response = model.prompt(messages=[
    system("You are a helpful pirate."),
    user("What is the capital of France?"),
    assistant("Paris, matey."),
    user("And Germany?"),
])
print(response.text())
LLM 以前从每个提示词返回一个可迭代的字符串序列。当模型返回字符串响应时，这非常有效，但未能预测模型未来会演变成的奇怪形态。如今，许多模型返回的是推理文本、输出字符串、工具调用甚至图像附件的混合体。在 LLM 0.32 中，你可以这样做：
结合这些功能，我们终于可以提供一个半标准 OpenAI 聊天补全 API 的稳健实现，我已将其作为 llm-chat-completions-server 插件发布：

llm install llm-chat-completions-server
llm chat-completions-server --port 9000
# Server is now running on http://127.0.0.1:9000/v1
现在你可以使用新的 llm openai endpoint 命令，通过该服务器对 LLM 运行提示词了！
llm openai endpoint http://127.0.0.1:9000/v1 'hello' -m gpt-5.4-mini
这种 API 的更大挑战在于日志记录。如果我们要支持在每次请求时追加消息序列的模式，理想情况下，我们应该避免为每一轮记录所有重复的 JSON。
解决方案是新的内容寻址消息存储，它是模仿 Git 设计的。你可以在文档中看到它的新架构，但 llm logs 和 llm logs --json 命令都已升级，能够将该格式转换回易于消费的内容。
其他内容
本次发布还有很多其他内容。0.32 的发布说明非常全面，而 0.32rc2、0.32rc、0.32a3、0.32a2 和 0.32a0 的说明应该可以填补任何遗漏。
现有的 LLM 插件应该都能继续工作，但提供额外模型的插件需要升级到 0.32，才能完全参与新的流式事件系统。文档中有一份关于使用结构化消息和流式事件实现插件的指南。
我更新了自己的一些插件：
llm-anthropic 0.26 增加了对 Claude 5 系列模型的支持，以及 WebSearch、WebFetch、CodeExecution 和 AnthropicMCP 服务端工具。
llm-gemini、llm-openrouter 和 llm-mistral 也快完成了，即将发布。
我想 LLM 现在已经是一个 agent 框架了
本次发布中相当一部分底层工具的改动是由 Datasette Agent 的需求驱动的。当我开始开发 LLM 时，“agent”这个词的定义非常模糊，以至于我拒绝使用它。到了 2025 年 9 月，我开始接受这样一个观点：“LLM agent 在循环中运行工具以实现目标”现在已经足够成熟，我可以不再完全回避这个词了。
工具链现在可以暂停以等待人工批准，并从存储的消息历史记录中恢复——这两点都是 Datasette Agent 所需要的。
现在看看 LLM，它在我眼中开始变得非常有 agent 的样子了。拥有一个 CLI 实用程序，能够将来自不同来源的不同工具与不同模型混合搭配，且全部通过单行命令完成，并且包含一个足够强大的 Python 库来构建像 Datasette Agent 和 llm-coding-agent 这样的系统，这确实很棒。
也许 LLM 的下一个版本会将“agent”的概念直接融入核心库中。我仍在思考那会是什么样子。

blocks.text: Open letters about AI development
I wrote this summary of the past few weeks of open letters as a section of my sponsors-only newsletter but I've decided to share it here as well.

Open Weights and American AI Leadership was shepherded by Microsoft, dated July 24th, and signed by 235 AI-adjacent companies including NVIDIA (see Jensen's first ever tweet), Amazon, Y Combinator, The Linux Foundation, and (a later signer) OpenAI.

It's clearly an argument designed to counter any instincts by the current US government to ban or limit open weight models over "safety" concerns - a reasonable consideration given what happened to Claude Fable 5!

Relying solely on closed models is not inherently safe: they can be breached, misused, or fail in ways that outsiders cannot detect. And concentrating advanced AI capabilities behind a small number of closed models compounds that risk. It results in a small number of single points of failure, weakens competition, and leaves critical technology in the hands of a few providers. Open weight models, on the other hand, allow a broad community of researchers and developers to examine their behavior, identify vulnerabilities, develop safeguards, and improve them over time.
The one surprising note in the letter is that it comes out in support of distillation, where models train on output from other models:

In shaping this ecosystem, policymakers should be careful not to conflate legitimate model-development techniques with misappropriation. Distillation, or the practice of using one model’s outputs to help train or improve another, is a widely used technique for model improvement, evaluation, and validation. It reflects a long tradition of learning from, building upon, and improving existing technologies, a tradition that has helped drive innovation since the rise of the open-source software movement.

Notably absent from the signatures: Anthropic, who published their own response Our position on open-weights models three days later. CEO Dario Amodei doubled down on the risk of authoritarian governments building "AI models that are more powerful than those built by the US", and models being "misused to carry out cyberattacks or biological attacks", and called for "a crack down on industrial-scale distillation operations", while also stating that "Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models".

Then on July 28th Pacing the Frontier was published, featuring signatures from "1,324 employees of frontier AI companies" - with names like Jakub Pachocki (Chief Scientist, OpenAI), Ilya Sutskever (Safe Superintelligence Inc, previously OpenAI), Dario Amodei (Anthropic), Jack Clark (Anthropic) and more. Their core message:
We request that the U.S. government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.

Their concern is intense competitive pressure combined with accelerated AI progress caused by automated AI research - and given that Anthropic produce 80% of their code with Claude Code, OpenAI had Sol reduce their end-to-end serving costs by 20%, and Kimi K3 designed a chip to serve a nano model built on its own architecture, you can see why people are taking that risk more seriously right now.

translations: 关于 AI 发展的公开信
我把过去几周关于公开信的总结写成了赞助者专属通讯的一个部分，但我决定也在这里分享出来。
《开放权重与美国 AI 领导力》由 Microsoft 牵头，日期为 7 月 24 日，共有 235 家与 AI 相关的公司签署，包括 NVIDIA（参见 Jensen 的第一条推文）、Amazon、Y Combinator、The Linux Foundation，以及（后来的签署者）OpenAI。
这显然是一个旨在反驳当前美国政府出于“安全”考虑而禁止或限制开放权重模型本能的论点——考虑到 Claude Fable 5 发生的事情，这是一个合理的考量！
仅仅依赖闭源模型本身并不安全：它们可能会被攻破、滥用，或者以局外人无法察觉的方式发生故障。将先进的 AI 能力集中在少数闭源模型背后会加剧这种风险。这会导致少数单点故障，削弱竞争，并将关键技术掌握在少数提供商手中。另一方面，开放权重模型允许广泛的研究人员和开发者社区检查其行为，识别漏洞，开发安全防护措施，并随着时间的推移对其进行改进。
这封信中令人惊讶的一点是，它公开支持蒸馏技术，即模型基于其他模型的输出进行训练：
在塑造这一生态系统时，政策制定者应小心，不要将合法的模型开发技术与盗用混为一谈。蒸馏，即使用一个模型的输出来帮助训练或改进另一个模型的做法，是一种广泛用于模型改进、评估和验证的技术。它反映了从现有技术中学习、在其基础上构建并加以改进的悠久传统，这一传统自开源软件运动兴起以来一直推动着创新。
签名中明显缺席的是 Anthropic，他们在三天后发表了自己的回应《我们对开放权重模型的立场》。CEO Dario Amodei 强调了威权政府构建“比美国构建的更强大的 AI 模型”的风险，以及模型被“滥用于实施网络攻击或生物攻击”的风险，并呼吁“打击工业规模的蒸馏操作”，同时声称“Anthropic 从未主张禁止开放权重模型”。
随后在 7 月 28 日，《把握前沿节奏》发表，署名者包括“1,324 名前沿 AI 公司的员工”——其中包括 Jakub Pachocki（OpenAI 首席科学家）、Ilya Sutskever（Safe Superintelligence Inc，前 OpenAI）、Dario Amodei（Anthropic）、Jack Clark（Anthropic）等人。他们的核心信息是：
我们请求美国政府支持一项国际努力，以开发有意识地把握自动化 AI 发展前沿所需的技术和治理工具。
他们担心的是激烈的竞争压力与自动化 AI 研究导致的 AI 进步加速相结合——考虑到 Anthropic 用 Claude Code 生成了他们 80% 的代码，OpenAI 让 Sol 将其端到端服务成本降低了 20%，而 Kimi K3 设计了一款芯片来服务于基于其自身架构构建的 nano 模型，你就能明白为什么人们现在更加严肃地对待这种风险了。

topPicks.title: I'm (mostly) picking models on speed now, not intelligence
topPicks.titleZh: I'm (mostly) picking models on speed now, not intelligence
topPicks.summary: I'm (mostly) picking models on speed now, not intelligence

blocks.text: For the first time I can remember, I'm not choosing my daily driver models on raw intelligence. I'm choosing them on speed.
Have we reached an intelligence tipping point?

This is probably going to age like spoilt milk, but right now, models around the ~Opus 4.6 level seem to be 'smart enough' for most of my daily tasks - code, pulling together research, designing slide decks and doing analytical tasks against a plethora of databases.

While like most I was hyped to play around with Fable, ironically the US Gov shutdown gave everyone time to get used to Opus again. When Fable came back post-hype with additional guardrails, the first thing I noticed was just how slow it is[1]. So slow, actually, that I switched back to Opus pretty quickly.

I've spent a lot of my career making software fast. It's remarkable how much better software feels to interact with when it's fast. In my experience (and many studies), you can take the most beautiful product, but if it's slow, you won't enjoy using it. Equally, you can take a very basic product that's super fast and it will feel brilliantly utilitarian. [2]

It's clear to me that when only a few, big, slow models cleared the aforementioned (and hypothetical) intelligence bar, it wasn't worth the trade off really to use a slower model. Whatever speed you gain you quickly lose in having to redo it because it was broken.
Is 100tok/s the new 100ms?
I've written before about agents feeling like dialup, back when frontier models were crawling along at 30-60tok/s. That has changed faster than I expected.

The key fact I remember is that to humans, ~100ms feels 'instant', the gold standard. I reckon 100tok/s output on a model is about as fast as I can keep up with. After that, it comes in faster than I can (skim) read. This isn't an exact bar, because increasingly most of the model time is spent in reasoning, and not actually showing you output tokens. And also it massively varies on your output, prose gets output with far fewer tokens per character than code, so your mileage may (and will) vary.

But roughly, 100-200tok/s to me seems pretty damn fast. Below 50tok/s output feels increasingly slow. Ironically, going past 200tok/s seems almost unnerving - you can try a model out here at 10,000tok/s+ (!). I'm sure this feeling will edge upwards as we get used to it and push our agents to do more complicated work.

Given the plethora of new models that I think are ~clearing the aforementioned bar - such as GLM5.2 and DeepSeek V4 Flash GA - that are open weights and small(er), we now have a wide range of models and speed. If you look at the speed rankings of various providers for GLM5.2 on OpenRouter you can see the enormous range of serving speed - from less than 30tok/s at the bottom to 129tok/s at the top.

This is another huge plus to the open weights ecosystem. While there are great benefits in cost that are obvious, the fact that providers are also incentivised to compete on speed like this is really interesting.[3]
But there are limitations
If you're familiar with Pareto's Principle and Amdahl's Law you'll know what's coming up.
Assuming "good enough" models continue to get faster and faster, increasingly the speed benefit is lost to tool calls, and us humans overseeing them.

Take an agent using a model processing at 50tok/s. Most of the time is spent waiting for inference to come back. Now run the same turn at 250tok/s and you'll see that increasingly you are bottlenecked on tool calls on your "local" machine and your decision making.
Rough numbers, but the shape holds. The 5x speedup on the model only buys you a 2x speedup on the turn, because the other 25 seconds didn't move.

And even worse, making your local machine faster on these tool calls is sort of stalling out, because hardware costs have gone parabolic because of AI. Yet again another weird derivative effect of the AI market.

So I suspect (for now at least) there is a limit to how much demand there will be for speed, past a certain point. No doubt there'll be some examples where huge amounts of reasoning are useful (like mathematics research), and speeding that up is helpful. But I'd expect many agents to start getting bottlenecked on your local/internal hardware, database calls and other bits of latency.
The price war is coming

Interestingly OpenAI reduced the cost of their Luna variant by 80% just before the DeepSeek V4 Flash GA release, making it remarkably affordable for a frontier model. While I haven't had as much luck with getting great output out of it vs GLM5.2, I think it points towards an absolute bloodbath of pricing at this end of the market.
You can see this happening on OpenRouter with GLM5.2 - endless discounts being offered to try and attract customers in. We're already down to $0.42/$1.32/MTok on GLM5.2 - 5% of the price of Opus.
While the very cheapest is slow, for not much more you can get 109tok/s from DeepInfra.

As the next generation set of GPUs start being deployed over the next few months - Nvidia's Vera Rubin series and AMD's MI400s, amongst others - the new HBM4 memory in those chips will deliver a 2x+ speedup on output tokens from memory bandwidth alone, plus more on top from additional compute and interlink.

In 2027 it's very possible we'll have very good quality models, at reasonable prices running at 500tok/s+. Staring at "still thinking on xhigh effort" for most of your day may finally become a thing of the past.

What will be interesting to watch for - and I'm not sure where to bet - is if the vast 2-3T+ param models actually do perform dramatically better for everyday tasks. On one hand it feels like we've hit a sweet spot right now, on another having an order of magnitude more intelligence in the model may make that sweet spot look very, very primitive.

Second of course is the endless guardrails firing, which tend to happen at the worst possible time - just when I'm getting deep into a difficult task and I feel I could do with the extra "firepower" that Fable offers, but that's a story for another day. ↩︎

A classic example is something like Craigslist or Hacker News. While they look dated, they are so damn responsive you don't notice. Equally, your "standard" SPA app serving 30MB of React to render a homepage feels like treacle and a chore to use most of the time, despite what was surely an enormous spend on design and product. ↩︎

I'm aware that both OpenAI and Anthropic have offered fast variants of models for a long time, but the API pricing is eye watering. Unless you are tokenmaxxing your benchmarks with a blank cheque, I haven't come across anyone that uses them for day to day operation. Having great models that are super fast at a reasonable price is a very recent addition to the market. ↩︎

translations: 在我记忆中，这是我第一次不根据原始智能来选择日常主力模型，而是根据速度来选择。
我们是否已经达到了智能的临界点？
这句话可能很快就会像变质牛奶一样过时，但就目前而言，智能水平在 Opus 4.6 左右的模型似乎已经“足够聪明”，可以胜任我大部分的日常任务——编写代码、汇总研究、设计幻灯片，以及针对大量数据库进行分析任务。
虽然和大多数人一样，我对试用 Fable 感到兴奋，但讽刺的是，美国政府的停摆给了大家重新适应 Opus 的时间。当 Fable 在热度消退后带着额外的护栏回归时，我注意到的第一件事就是它太慢了[1]。实际上，它慢到我很快就切回了 Opus。
我的职业生涯中有很多时间都在致力于让软件变快。当软件运行迅速时，交互体验的提升是显而易见的。根据我的经验（以及许多研究），即使是最精美的产品，如果运行缓慢，你也不会喜欢使用它。同样，一个非常基础但速度极快的产品，也会让人感觉极其好用。[2]
我很清楚，当只有少数几个庞大且缓慢的模型能够达到前述（假设的）智能标准时，使用较慢的模型其实并不值得。你获得的任何速度优势，都会因为模型出错而不得不重做，从而迅速丧失。
100tok/s 是新的 100ms 吗？
我以前写过，当前沿模型还在以 30-60tok/s 的速度缓慢爬行时，智能体感觉就像拨号上网一样。这种情况改变得比我预期的要快。

我记得的一个关键事实是，对人类来说，大约 100ms 的延迟感觉就是“瞬间”的，这是黄金标准。我认为模型 100tok/s 的输出速度大约是我能跟上的极限。超过这个速度，它的输出就比我（略读）的速度还要快了。这并不是一个精确的标准，因为现在模型的大部分时间都花在了推理上，而不是实际向你展示输出的 token。而且这也很大程度上取决于你的输出内容，散文每个字符输出的 token 数量比代码少得多，所以你的实际体验可能会有所不同。
但大致来说，100-200tok/s 对我来说已经相当快了。低于 50tok/s 的输出会让人感觉越来越慢。讽刺的是，超过 200tok/s 似乎反而让人有些不安——你可以在这里试试 10,000tok/s+ (!) 的模型。我确信，随着我们逐渐习惯这种速度并推动智能体处理更复杂的工作，这种感觉的阈值也会逐渐提高。
鉴于我认为有许多新模型已经达到了前述标准——例如 GLM5.2 和 DeepSeek V4 Flash GA——它们是开放权重且体积较小，我们现在拥有了丰富的模型和速度选择。如果你查看 OpenRouter 上各个提供商对 GLM5.2 的速度排名，你会发现服务速度的跨度极大——从底部的不到 30tok/s 到顶部的 129tok/s。
这是开放权重生态系统的另一个巨大优势。虽然成本上的好处显而易见，但提供商们同样有动力在速度上展开竞争，这确实非常有趣。[3]
但也存在局限性
如果你熟悉帕累托法则和阿姆达尔定律，你就会知道接下来会发生什么。
假设“足够好”的模型继续变得越来越快，那么速度优势将越来越多地消耗在工具调用以及我们人类对它们的监督上。
假设有一个使用处理速度为 50tok/s 的模型的智能体。大部分时间都花在等待推理返回上。现在以 250tok/s 的速度运行同一轮次，你会发现越来越明显的是，瓶颈转移到了“本地”机器上的工具调用以及你的决策过程上。
数字是粗略的，但整体趋势成立。模型速度提升 5 倍只能让单轮次速度提升 2 倍，因为另外那 25 秒并没有缩短。
更糟糕的是，在这些工具调用上提升本地机器的速度正陷入停滞，因为 AI 导致硬件成本呈抛物线般飙升。这又是 AI 市场带来的另一个奇怪的衍生效应。
因此我怀疑（至少目前是这样），对速度的需求在越过某个临界点后是有限的。毫无疑问，在某些场景下海量的推理是有用的（比如数学研究），加快推理速度也会有所帮助。但我预计许多智能体将开始在本地/内部硬件、数据库调用以及其他延迟上遇到瓶颈。
价格战即将打响
有趣的是，OpenAI 在 DeepSeek V4 Flash 正式发布前夕将其 Luna 变体的成本降低了 80%，使其作为一款前沿模型变得异常实惠。虽然与 GLM5.2 相比，我并没有从它那里获得出色输出的好运，但我认为这预示着这一端的市场将出现一场绝对的价格血战。
你可以在 OpenRouter 上的 GLM5.2 看到这种情况——不断提供折扣以试图吸引客户。GLM5.2 的价格已经降到了 $0.42/$1.32/MTok——仅为 Opus 价格的 5%。
虽然最便宜的选项速度很慢，但只需多花一点点钱，你就可以从 DeepInfra 获得 109tok/s 的速度。
随着下一代 GPU 在未来几个月内开始部署——包括 Nvidia 的 Vera Rubin 系列和 AMD 的 MI400s 等——这些芯片中的新 HBM4 内存仅凭内存带宽就能在输出 token 上带来 2 倍以上的速度提升，再加上额外的计算和互连，提升还会更多。
到了 2027 年，我们很有可能拥有质量极高、价格合理且运行速度超过 500tok/s 的模型。一天中大部分时间都盯着“仍在以极高算力思考”的状态，可能终于要成为历史了。
值得关注的一件趣事——我也不确定该押注哪一边——是那些庞大的 2-3T+ 参数模型在日常任务中是否真的表现得显著更好。一方面，感觉我们现在已经达到了一个最佳平衡点；另一方面，模型中多出一个数量级的智能可能会让这个平衡点显得非常、非常原始。
其次当然是没完没了的安全护栏触发，这往往发生在最糟糕的时候——正当我深入一项困难任务，觉得我正需要 Fable 提供的额外“火力”时，但这又是另一回事了。 ↩︎
一个经典的例子是 Craigslist 或 Hacker News 这样的网站。虽然它们看起来过时了，但响应速度快得惊人，以至于你根本注意不到。同样，你那些“标准”的 SPA 应用为了渲染一个首页要加载 30MB 的 React，大部分时间用起来就像在糖浆里跋涉一样费劲，尽管它们在设计上和产品上肯定投入了巨大的开销。 ↩︎
我知道 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 很久以前就提供过模型的快速变体，但它们的 API 定价令人咋舌。除非你拿着空头支票在基准测试中疯狂刷 token，否则我还没见过谁在日常运营中使用它们。拥有价格合理且速度超快的优秀模型，是最近才加入市场的。 ↩︎

blocks.text: Written with LLM assistance.Details at end.

I’ve been meaning to write an update on how Compiler Explorer actually runs on Amazon’s cloud, and it’s been sat on my list for a good while now, somewhere behind the other random things that take up what laughably I refer to as my spare time1.

The last time I wrote about this was 2016, when the whole site was a load balancer, a couple of instances and some Docker containers I built on my laptop. I wrote a much longer how it works last summer, but that one is mostly about Compiler Explorer and only incidentally about the cloud it sits on.

It’s no secret that we run on AWS, and none of it is hidden: the infra repository has all the terraform, the install scripts and the ce command line tool we drive the whole thing with, so if you’d rather read the real thing than my description of it, help yourself. So this one goes the other way round, through the Amazon services we lean on, roughly in the order your compile request runs into them.
Getting your code as far as our servers

Your browser talks to CloudFront, Amazon’s CDN. We run two separate CloudFront distributions. The one in front of godbolt.org mostly just hands requests on to our load balancer, caching what it sensibly can and compressing things on the way back out2. The bulky static stuff lives in an S3 bucket behind a second distribution at static.ce-cdn.net: the compiled JavaScript, the images, the web fonts. Much the largest part of that is Monaco, the editor component out of Visual Studio Code, which is what gives you the syntax highlighting and the squiggly underlines and the rest of it. It’s a lot of JavaScript to send someone who only wants to look at some assembly, so it’s worth having it cached near them.

Sitting in front of that is WAF, doing our rate limiting. Our limits are very simple and very high, mostly because we used to be stricter and it kept catching C++ trainers: a whole classroom behind a conference’s NAT looks like a single very keen IP address. We could probably do something cleverer with fingerprinting, but raising the limit was easier and it hasn’t been a problem since.3
Rather a lot of fleets behind one load balancer

Behind CloudFront is a single Application Load Balancer. It works out from the path which cluster a request is for, and then picks a healthy instance in that cluster to send it to. Almost everything has no special prefix at all and goes to the production fleet, which is where the overwhelming bulk of the traffic ends up. /beta* and /staging* go to the beta and staging fleets4. /winprod* goes to a fleet of Windows instances running MSVC, /aarch64prod* to Graviton machines that run ARM code natively rather than under emulation, and /gpu* to machines with real NVIDIA cards in them5.

Each of those is an Auto Scaling Group, and these days each one is doubled up: a blue and a green. To deploy, we bring up the other colour, wait for it to go healthy, point the load balancer’s target group at it and drain the old one. If it’s wrong, we point it back. Before that, deploying meant a rolling restart of the fleet with our ce command line tool, one instance at a time. That worked well enough, but backing out a bad release meant rolling the whole fleet forward again onto the previous version, which is a bit slow when you’ve just broken the site.
The scaling itself is simple: we just try and keep the average CPU load below a threshold. We’ve kicked around more sophisticated ideas but this one is supported out of the box6.
Renting the bits nobody else wants

The production fleet is almost entirely spot instances – unused EC2 capacity, sold off cheap, on the understanding that you can be evicted at two minutes’ notice. It’s a 60-90% saving over on-demand – quite a lot of money, for us.

We can get away with that because our instances don’t really matter. Everything that needs to survive lives on the shared filesystem, in S3 or in DynamoDB, so an instance that vanishes is just an instance that gets replaced. We ask for sixteen different instance types across the m5, m6, m7, r6 and i3/i4i families. The allocation strategy is price-capacity-optimized – Amazon’s way of saying “pick whichever of these is cheapest and least likely to get yanked”. In practice we get evicted, the scaling group notices, and a new one turns up.
Why the compilers are the hard part

We have around 6,000 compiler entries9 across 93 languages, and we never delete any of them7. Once a compiler version goes up it stays up, so that Stack Overflow answer showing a GCC 4.8 codegen quirk still compiles today. It’s our bit against link rot, and it does mean we hoard an awful lot of binaries.

All of that lives on EFS, Amazon’s elastic NFS, and NFS has latency. C-like languages pull in an enormous number of very small header files, so the naive version of this is unusably slow. Our fix, which sounds daft, is to build a SquashFS image per compiler, store the image also on EFS, and mount it through a loopback device. The kernel then thinks it’s talking to a local block device and caches blocks properly instead of checking with a server in another building every time10.

That worked, but it meant mounting a couple of thousand images at every boot, which took the best part of a minute and kept the metadata for thousands of filesystems resident in kernel memory. That cached metadata is a good chunk of why squashfs beats NFS in the first place, so it’s not wasted as such; it’s just that any one instance is only ever going to touch a handful of those compilers, so we were paying for all of it to use a fraction of it. It took me three years and several abandoned attempts to fix that, and the answer was CEFS: content-addressed images, packed into bundles of around 20GB, mounted on demand by autofs the first time something touches the path. The migration took us from 2,182 images down to 121, and OS startup from 50 seconds to 20! It’s crept back up to around 883 since, because the nightly builds keep making new images and consolidation only packs down whatever is already there. A garbage collection while I was writing this turned up 111 images that nothing references any more, about 63GiB’s worth8.
Our storage has come down a lot over the year too, though I’m honestly not sure how much of that is CEFS and how much is me finally deleting the old squash images:

Aug/04 01:55 admin-node~ $ df -h
Filesystem                                 Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/nvme0n1p1                              97G   20G   77G  21% /
fs-db4c8192.efs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:/  8.0E  2.2T  8.0E   1% /opt
2.2T, where a year ago it was 3.9T. Still nowhere near 8 exabytes, mind.
Building compilers all night, every night

We build a pile of compilers from scratch every night: GCC trunk, Clang trunk, and a long tail of experimental branches for reflection, contracts, coroutines and all the other fun stuff. That’s 94 nightly build jobs at the moment11, up from 73 a year ago and 33 in 2022.

Those run on our own GitHub Actions runners on EC2, spun up on demand with the excellent terraform-aws-github-runner, with all the compiler orchestration on top being ours. Building trunk LLVM wants a big machine and a decent chunk of time, and GitHub’s hosted runners weren’t up to it when we set this up.
This is the part of the bill that goes up every time somebody asks us for another compiler and we say yes12.
The bits that are half-finished

One thing we’ve built but not finished rolling out is what we call the CE Router: a small fleet whose job is to decide where a compilation should happen, look the answer up in DynamoDB and drop the request on an SQS queue, with the result coming back to your browser over an API Gateway WebSocket. The point is to stop the machine that answers the HTTP request having to be the machine that owns the compiler.

It works, but it isn’t carrying production traffic yet: the load balancer rules that would send compilations through it are still commented out, and we’re migrating gradually. Your compile today still goes straight to a machine in the prod fleet, the way it always has.

Building it did turn up a good AWS gotcha, though. API Gateway WebSocket frames top out at 32KiB, and the assembly for almost any non-trivial program is bigger than that; in the other direction SQS messages cap out at 256KB, which a decent-sized multi-file project will go past. So in both directions, if the thing is too big we shove it in S3 and send a key instead.
Everything else
A scattering of other services doing one job each:
DynamoDB holds the short links. Every godbolt.org/z/... you’ve put in a slide deck is a row in a table, and there are a couple of million of them.
S3 holds the compilers we build, the static assets, the logs, and a daily-expiring content-addressable compilation cache, so the second person to compile the same thing gets it for free.
Lambda does the odd jobs: the Claude Explain backend, the nightly version tracking, and the one that pushes CloudWatch alarms into our Discord so it’s not just my phone buzzing at 3am.
Route 53, ACM, CloudTrail, Backup and SES are the plumbing. I don’t think about them much.
CloudWatch drives the auto-scaling triggers, though for actually looking at things we run Grafana, Prometheus and Loki. Those dashboards are public.

Everything is in us-east-1. If you’re compiling from Sydney your code goes a long way round, and I’m afraid it’s going to keep doing that: keeping a couple of terabytes of compilers in sync across regions would be an absolute nightmare.
Some numbers

We log a heavily anonymised JSON record to S3 for every compilation, with a Glue table over the top, so while writing this I went and counted them properly: 5,238,210 compilations in July, and 78.7 million over the last twelve months. It’s been sliding gently all year, down about a third from last autumn’s peak.
Compilations per month over the last year. Generated from this script.

The big drop before that, from 2024’s 14 million a month, I can at least half explain: in mid-2024 we doubled the default delay before we auto-recompile as you type, from 750ms to 1500ms, and then to 2 seconds13. If you type continuously, doubling that delay roughly halves the number of compilations you generate, without anybody noticing anything much. This latest slide isn’t that, though: it started well over a year later.

So I don’t really have a good explanation, and I can’t easily go and find one, because we deliberately don’t track who you are: no cookies, nothing that would let me tell you how many people used the site yesterday. I’d make that trade again every time, but it does leave me squinting at graphs occasionally.
Since I had the query open, here’s what folks actually compiled in July:

id                      compiles   compiler
g161                   1,386,532   GCC 16.1 (C++)
cg161                    403,659   GCC 16.1 (C)
gsnapshot                298,256   GCC trunk
clang_trunk              287,885   Clang trunk
g152                     239,331   GCC 15.2
clang2210                177,958   Clang 22.1
vcpp_v19_latest_x64      132,186   MSVC
r1970                     65,380   Rust 1.97
python314                 51,104   Python 3.14

That top entry is 26% of everything – roughly what you’d expect when you’re the default15. The load balancer sees around 14 million requests a month; our busiest day this year was the 21st of April at 1.44 million. The auto-scaling dealt with that one by itself; I only found out about it while writing this.

All of that costs us somewhere around $3,600 a month on AWS at the moment, which works out at about $0.0007 per compilation14. For the best part of a year we barely paid any of that: AWS’s open source credits covered almost all of it. Those ran out in the spring, we paid our own way for a few months, and AWS have just renewed them for another year, which is a huge help. Either way we’re fine for money, thanks to our Patreon supporters, our GitHub sponsors and our commercial sponsors. I did a full breakdown of the costs last year and it’s still roughly the right shape.
The wall of compilers, a year on: 6,157 entries across 93 languages.Regenerated from the same script as last year's.
Things I’d still like to fix

Deployment is better than it was but there’s still more hand-holding in it than I’d like16. The CE Router migration has been “nearly done” for a while now… I still wish I’d laid out the NFS directory structure properly at the start instead of growing it one compiler at a time for a decade. And we moved everything to Ubuntu 24.04 this year, which was not the tidy little upgrade it sounds like17.

None of this is especially clever: it’s a load balancer, some scaling groups full of cheap spot instances, a network filesystem and a decade of accumulated hacks. It does keep working, though, and these days it mostly keeps working without anyone having to go and poke it. I’m pretty happy with that.
Thanks

As ever, the people who keep this running are the contributors. Partouf (Patrick Quist) above all – I really don’t know what CE would do without them – along with the core team and the many, many people who send PRs and file issues. Thank you all. Thanks too to AWS, whose open source credits programme paid for the best part of a year of everything described above, and who have just renewed for another year – which is not a small thing for a project our size, and it lets us get on with the interesting problems instead of watching the bill. Thank you AWS! And thanks, as always, to our Patreon and GitHub Sponsors supporters and our commercial sponsors, who cover the rest.
Questions? Complaints? Compilers we’re missing? Drop by our Discord, or find me on Bluesky or Mastodon.
Disclaimer

This article was a collaboration between a human and an LLM. I set it off to dig through our infrastructure repositories and our AWS account for the current numbers, which turned up several things I had wrong, and worked from that. It also ran the Athena queries and regenerated the graphs. The opinions, em- and en-dashes, and mistakes are all mine.

In my defence, those have included a month back in the UK dealing with some family things, a run of C++ talks (C++Now, ACCU on Sea, CppCon, a keynote at C++ Under the Sea, and Meeting C++ in Berlin, where I’ll be going into a lot of this in rather more detail), some more Computerphile videos, and getting completely obsessed with how PAL decoding works. ↩
We only got round to turning brotli compression on at the edge for the main app in June this year. ↩

WAF also gives us a banned-ipv4 and a banned-ipv6 list that I add to by hand when we spot somebody misbehaving, and take them off again once they’ve got the hint. It doesn’t happen often: last year it was one anomalous IPv6 address, and an analytics outfit that was hammering us, who came off the list again the next day. Every now and again some enterprising soul works out that a site which compiles and runs arbitrary code is, if you squint, a free compute farm, but that’s rare and it tends to be pretty obvious. ↩
Beta is very rarely used, but when we do have a longer-term experiment on the go that’s where it lives. Staging is for short-lived pre-deploy checks. ↩

These cost a small fortune to run, but being able to see the results of running GPU code makes it worthwhile. We worked with our friends at NVIDIA to get the drivers and toolchains working properly, and they were a corporate sponsor for a good while too. Thank you NVIDIA! ↩

The obvious better signal is queue depth: how many compilations are actually waiting, rather than how busy the CPUs happen to look. We already have scaling policies written against ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible for some of the environments, and once the queue-based compilation path is carrying real traffic everywhere that’s what we’d like to scale everything on. ↩

Nearly never, anyway. Very occasionally an experimental build gets replaced, and the nightly builds replace themselves by definition: today’s GCC trunk quietly does away with yesterday’s. It’s the released versions that stay put forever. ↩

Content addressing does at least make that safe to work out: an image that nothing links to is definitely unused, so the collection can be automatic rather than me squinting at filenames and hoping. A good chunk of those 111 will be yesterday’s nightly builds, quietly superseded by today’s. ↩

6,157 if you ask the API, but that’s cheating slightly: it counts the same GCC once for C, once for C++, once for Fortran and so on. Unique names, it’s 4,291. Last June the equivalent numbers were 4,724 and 81 languages, so we’re still growing pretty nicely, and almost none of that is me: folks keep turning up with a language I’d never heard of and a working PR. ↩

Normally NFS caches data locally, but it still validates that cached metadata is fresh with the server via attribute caching. Even when the file data is cached you pay the network latency to check it hasn’t changed. Going via a loopback-mounted SquashFS image “launders” away the NFS-ness: the squashfs driver sees a local block device, and the kernel is blissfully unaware that behind those cached blocks is a file on NFS that could in theory change. For immutable compiler images this is a huge boon. ↩

A “job” isn’t a compiler: some build one thing, some build a whole family. The builds kick off at midnight UTC and queue on our build infrastructure, and a separate workflow installs at 5:30am, and the two still have no idea about each other, so sometimes we install yesterday’s builds. It’s on the list. ↩

We’re not completely daft about it: before a nightly build runs it checks whether any of the upstream repositories have had a commit in the last week, and if nothing’s moved it skips the build entirely. A quiet week on some experimental branch costs us nothing much. ↩
#6669, if you want the gory details. It went out at 1500ms, then someone tried 2 seconds, then it got reverted, then it went back to 2 seconds ten days later. The current default is 2000ms. ↩

Up from $0.00039 a year ago, and not because anything got dearer. The volume went down and the fixed costs – all that storage, and building all those compilers every night – stayed exactly where they were. ↩

I did this same exercise back in 2014, out of nearly 2 million compiles in total, to work out whether I could retire GCC 4.4. The default then was clang++ 3.0.6 at 37%, so the shape of the list hasn’t changed much even if everything else has. I didn’t retire GCC 4.4, and it’s still there. ↩

Mainly it’s our “compiler discovery” step: before a version goes out we go and ask every compiler on the machine what it actually is and what it calls itself, and write the answers to a JSON file the site then reads. It’s still a manual step and it can occasionally fall over, though I think I’ve made it rather more stable in a recent commit. I’m also experimenting with using LLM “scripts” to help where I can’t automate things directly in code: there are a lot of weird edge cases to handle and encoding all of them properly is tricky. ↩

Modern glibc uses SHT_RELR relocations, which need binutils 2.38 or newer to link against, and 29 of our older GCCs ship their own ld that predates that. We tried rebuilding them all from source, which cascaded into a wall of libsanitizer incompatibilities, so we gave up and settled for symlinking those compilers’ ld to a newer one at install time instead. Partouf later rebuilt a couple of them properly. ↩

translations: 本文在 LLM 的协助下撰写。详情见文末。
我一直想写篇文章更新一下 Compiler Explorer 实际上是如何在亚马逊云上运行的，这件事在我的待办清单上已经躺了很长一段时间了，排在了其他那些占据了我戏称为“业余时间”的杂事之后1。
我上次写这个话题是在 2016 年，当时整个网站就是一个负载均衡器、几个实例以及一些我在笔记本上构建的 Docker 容器。去年夏天我写了一篇长得多的关于其工作原理的文章，但那篇主要讲的是 Compiler Explorer，只是偶然提到了它所依托的云平台。
我们在 AWS 上运行并不是什么秘密，而且没有任何隐藏：基础设施仓库里有所有的 terraform 代码、安装脚本以及我们用来驱动整个系统的 ce 命令行工具，所以如果你更愿意看真实的东西而不是我的描述，请自便。因此，这篇文章换个角度，按照你的编译请求所遇到的顺序，大致介绍一下我们所依赖的亚马逊服务。
将你的代码传输到我们的服务器

你的浏览器与 CloudFront（亚马逊的 CDN）进行通信。我们运行了两个独立的 CloudFront 分配。godbolt.org 前面的那个主要只是将请求转发给我们的负载均衡器，在合理的情况下进行缓存，并在返回时进行压缩2。庞大的静态内容存放在 static.ce-cdn.net 上第二个分配背后的一个 S3 存储桶中：包括编译后的 JavaScript、图像和网络字体。其中最大的一部分是 Monaco，即 Visual Studio Code 的编辑器组件，它为你提供了语法高亮、波浪下划线以及其他功能。对于只想看一些汇编代码的人来说，发送这么多 JavaScript 是相当多的，因此值得在靠近他们的地方进行缓存。
在它前面的是 WAF，负责我们的速率限制。我们的限制非常简单而且阈值很高，主要是因为我们以前比较严格，结果总是误伤 C++ 培训师：整个教室在一个会议的 NAT 后面，看起来就像是一个极其活跃的单个 IP 地址。我们或许可以通过指纹识别做一些更聪明的处理，但提高限制阈值更容易，而且从那以后这就不再是问题了。3
一个负载均衡器背后相当多的集群

CloudFront 背后是一个单一的 Application Load Balancer。它根据路径判断请求属于哪个集群，然后在该集群中选择一个健康的实例来发送请求。几乎所有内容都没有特殊前缀，并会进入生产集群，这也是绝大多数流量最终的去向。/beta* 和 /staging* 分别进入 beta 和 staging 集群4。/winprod* 进入运行 MSVC 的 Windows 实例集群，/aarch64prod* 进入原生运行 ARM 代码而非模拟运行的 Graviton 机器，而 /gpu* 则进入装有真实 NVIDIA 显卡的机器5。

其中的每一个都是一个 Auto Scaling Group，而且现在每个都加倍了：一个蓝色和一个绿色。为了部署，我们启动另一种颜色，等待其状态变为健康，将负载均衡器的目标组指向它，然后排空旧的。如果出错了，我们就指回去。在此之前，部署意味着使用我们的 ce 命令行工具对集群进行滚动重启，一次一个实例。这虽然足够好用，但回滚一个糟糕的版本意味着将整个集群再次向前滚动到上一个版本，当你刚刚弄坏了网站时，这有点慢。
扩展本身很简单：我们只是试图将平均 CPU 负载保持在阈值以下。我们曾讨论过更复杂的想法，但这个方案是开箱即支持的6。
租用没人想要的计算资源
生产环境集群几乎全部使用竞价型实例（spot instances）——即闲置的 EC2 容量，以低价出售，前提是你可能会在收到两分钟通知后被驱逐。与按需实例相比，这能节省 60-90% 的成本——对我们来说，这是一笔不小的数目。

我们能这么做是因为我们的实例其实并不重要。所有需要持久化的数据都存放在共享文件系统、S3 或 DynamoDB 中，所以一个实例消失只是意味着它会被替换。我们请求了 m5、m6、m7、r6 和 i3/i4i 系列中的 16 种不同实例类型。分配策略是 price-capacity-optimized（价格容量优化）——亚马逊的说法是“挑选其中最便宜且最不容易被收回的实例”。在实际运行中，如果我们被驱逐，扩展组会注意到，然后一个新的实例就会出现。
为什么编译器是最棘手的部分
我们有涵盖 93 种语言的约 6,000 个编译器条目9，而且我们从不删除它们7。一旦某个编译器版本上线，它就会一直保留，这样那个展示 GCC 4.8 代码生成特性的 Stack Overflow 回答今天依然可以编译。这是我们对抗链接失效（link rot）的一点努力，但这确实意味着我们囤积了海量的二进制文件。
所有这些都存放在 EFS（亚马逊的弹性 NFS）上，而 NFS 存在延迟。类 C 语言会引入大量非常小的头文件，所以最直接的做法会慢得无法使用。我们的解决办法听起来有点傻：为每个编译器构建一个 SquashFS 镜像，同样存放在 EFS 上，然后通过环回设备（loopback device）挂载它。这样内核就会认为它在与本地块设备通信，并正确地缓存块，而不是每次都去和另一栋楼里的服务器确认10。

这招奏效了，但这意味着每次启动都要挂载几千个镜像，这大约需要一分钟的时间，并且会让数千个文件系统的元数据常驻在内核内存中。这些缓存的元数据正是 squashfs 能够胜过 NFS 的重要原因，所以这并没有浪费；只是任何一个实例实际上只会用到其中一小部分编译器，所以我们为了使用其中一小部分而付出了全部的代价。我花了三年时间和几次放弃的尝试才解决这个问题，答案是 CEFS：内容寻址的镜像，打包成约 20GB 的捆绑包，在首次访问路径时由 autofs 按需挂载。这次迁移将我们的镜像数量从 2,182 个减少到了 121 个，操作系统启动时间从 50 秒缩短到了 20 秒！从那以后，这个数字又慢慢回升到了 883 个左右，因为每日构建不断生成新镜像，而合并操作只能压缩已有的内容。就在我写这篇文章时进行的一次垃圾回收发现了 111 个不再被任何东西引用的镜像，价值约 63GiB8。
过去一年里，我们的存储量也大幅下降，尽管说实话，我不确定这其中有多少归功于 CEFS，又有多少是因为我终于删除了旧的 squash 镜像：

Aug/04 01:55 admin-node~ $ df -h
Filesystem                                 Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/nvme0n1p1                              97G   20G   77G  21% /
fs-db4c8192.efs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:/  8.0E  2.2T  8.0E   1% /opt
现在是 2.2T，而一年前是 3.9T。不过请注意，这离 8 艾字节（exabytes）还差得远。
每天晚上通宵构建编译器
我们每天晚上都会从头构建一大批编译器：GCC trunk、Clang trunk，以及用于反射、契约、协程和其他各种有趣功能的实验性分支的长尾。目前有 94 个每日构建任务11，而一年前是 73 个，2022 年是 33 个。
这些任务运行在 EC2 上我们自己的 GitHub Actions runners 上，通过出色的 terraform-aws-github-runner 按需启动，而顶层的所有编译器编排工作都由我们自己完成。构建主干 LLVM 需要大型机器和相当长的时间，而在我们搭建这套系统时，GitHub 托管的 runners 根本无法胜任。
这部分账单每次都会上涨，因为每当有人要求我们添加另一个编译器并且我们同意时12，成本就会增加。
半成品部分
我们已经构建但尚未完全推出的是我们称之为 CE Router 的东西：一个小型集群，其工作是决定编译应该在哪里进行，在 DynamoDB 中查找答案，并将请求放入 SQS 队列，然后结果通过 API Gateway WebSocket 返回到您的浏览器。关键在于，让响应 HTTP 请求的机器不必再是拥有编译器的机器。
它可以运行，但尚未承载生产流量：将编译任务发送到这里的负载均衡器规则仍然被注释掉了，我们正在逐步迁移。您今天的编译仍然像往常一样直接进入生产集群中的机器。
不过，构建它确实遇到了一个 AWS 的坑。API Gateway WebSocket 帧的上限是 32KiB，而几乎所有非平凡程序的汇编代码都会超过这个大小；在另一个方向上，SQS 消息的上限是 256KB，一个规模可观的跨文件项目也会超过这个限制。因此，在双向传输中，如果内容太大，我们就把它塞进 S3 并发送一个 key。
其他一切
一些零散的其他服务，每个服务只做一件事：
DynamoDB 存储短链接。你放在幻灯片里的每一个 godbolt.org/z/... 都是表中的一行，这样的链接有几百万个。
S3 存储我们构建的编译器、静态资源、日志，以及一个每天过期、基于内容寻址的编译缓存，这样第二个编译相同内容的人就可以免费获得结果。
Lambda 负责处理杂项任务：Claude Explain 后端、每夜版本跟踪，以及将 CloudWatch 警报推送到我们 Discord 的任务，这样凌晨 3 点响起的就不只是我的手机了。
Route 53、ACM、CloudTrail、Backup 和 SES 是基础设施。我平时很少去想它们。
CloudWatch 驱动自动扩缩容触发器，不过为了实际查看情况，我们运行了 Grafana、Prometheus 和 Loki。这些仪表板是公开的。
一切都位于 us-east-1。如果你从悉尼进行编译，你的代码要绕很远的路，而且恐怕会一直这样：跨区域同步几 TB 的编译器绝对是一场噩梦。
一些数字
我们为每次编译向 S3 记录一条高度匿名化的 JSON 记录，并在其上建立 Glue 表，因此在写这篇文章时，我专门去仔细数了一下：7 月份有 5,238,210 次编译，过去十二个月有 7870 万次。这个数字全年都在缓慢下降，比去年秋天的峰值下降了约三分之一。
过去一年的每月编译量。由该脚本生成。
在此之前的大幅下降，从 2024 年每月 1400 万次下降，我至少能解释一半：在 2024 年年中，我们将你输入时自动重新编译的默认延迟翻倍，从 750ms 增加到 1500ms，然后又增加到 2 秒13。如果你连续输入，将延迟翻倍大约会使你生成的编译次数减半，而几乎没有人会注意到。不过，最近的这次下降并非如此：它是在一年多之后才开始的。
所以我确实没有一个很好的解释，而且我也很难去找到一个，因为我们刻意不去追踪你是谁：没有 cookies，也没有任何东西能让我告诉你昨天有多少人使用了这个网站。每次我都会做出同样的取舍，但这确实偶尔会让我对着图表发呆。
既然我已经打开了查询，以下是大家在七月份实际编译的内容：

g161                   1,386,532   GCC 16.1 (C++)
cg161                    403,659   GCC 16.1 (C)

clang_trunk              287,885   Clang trunk

clang2210                177,958   Clang 22.1
vcpp_v19_latest_x64      132,186   MSVC

排在最前面的那个条目占了总量的 26%——这大概就是当你作为默认选项15时所期望的比例。负载均衡器每个月大约会接收到 1400 万次请求；今年我们最忙的一天是 4 月 21 日，达到了 144 万次。自动扩缩容自己处理了那次高峰；我只是在写这篇文章时才发现这件事。

目前所有这些在 AWS 上每月大约花费我们 3600 美元，折算下来每次编译大约 0.0007 美元14。在将近一年的时间里，我们几乎没有为此付过钱：AWS 的开源额度几乎覆盖了全部费用。这些额度在春天用完了，我们自掏腰包支付了几个月，而 AWS 刚刚又为我们续订了一年，这帮了大忙。无论如何，我们的资金状况都还不错，这要感谢我们的 Patreon 支持者、GitHub 赞助商以及我们的商业赞助商。我去年做过一次详细的成本明细，现在的大致情况依然如此。
一年后的编译器墙：涵盖 93 种语言的 6157 个条目。由与去年相同的脚本重新生成。
我仍然想修复的问题
部署比以前好多了，但其中仍然有比我预想中更多的手动干预16。CE Router 的迁移已经“快完成了”有一阵子了……我仍然希望一开始就能把 NFS 目录结构规划好，而不是十年来每次增加一个编译器就让它膨胀一点。而且今年我们把所有东西都迁移到了 Ubuntu 24.04，这并不像听起来那样是一次轻松的小升级17。
这些都没有特别巧妙的地方：就是一个负载均衡器，一些装满廉价竞价型实例的扩缩容组，一个网络文件系统，以及十年来积累的各种 hack。不过它确实一直在运行，而且现在大多数时候都不需要任何人去干预它就能保持工作。对此我相当满意。
致谢

一如既往，让这一切保持运转的是贡献者们。尤其是 Partouf (Patrick Quist)——我真的不知道如果没有他们 CE 会变成什么样——还有核心团队以及许许多多发送 PR 和提交 issue 的人。谢谢大家。还要感谢 AWS，他们的开源额度计划为上述几乎所有内容支付了将近一年的费用，而且刚刚又续订了一年——对于我们这种规模的项目来说，这绝不是一件小事，它让我们可以专注于解决有趣的问题，而不是盯着账单发愁。谢谢 AWS！一如既往地，还要感谢我们的 Patreon 和 GitHub Sponsors 支持者以及我们的商业赞助商，他们承担了其余的费用。
有问题？有抱怨？有我们遗漏的编译器？欢迎来我们的 Discord 看看，或者在 Bluesky 和 Mastodon 上找我。
免责声明
这篇文章是人类和 LLM 合作完成的。我让它去挖掘我们的基础设施代码库和 AWS 账户以获取最新数据，这发现了我记错的几个地方，并在此基础上进行了修正。它还运行了 Athena 查询并重新生成了图表。其中的观点、破折号以及错误全都是我的。
为我辩护一下，这些原因包括回英国一个月处理一些家庭事务，一系列的 C++ 演讲（C++Now、ACCU on Sea、CppCon、在 C++ Under the Sea 上的主题演讲，以及柏林的 Meeting C++，我会在那里更详细地探讨其中很多内容），制作了更多 Computerphile 视频，以及完全沉迷于研究 PAL 解码的工作原理。
直到今年 6 月，我们才抽出时间在边缘节点为主应用开启了 brotli 压缩。

WAF 还为我们提供了一个 banned-ipv4 和一个 banned-ipv6 列表，当我们发现有人行为不端时，我会手动将他们添加进去，等他们明白过来后再将他们移除。这种情况并不常见：去年是一个异常的 IPv6 地址，以及一家对我们进行猛烈请求的分析公司，他们在第二天就被移出了列表。偶尔会有一些精明的人发现，一个可以编译和运行任意代码的网站，如果你眯起眼睛看，就是一个免费的算力农场，但这很罕见，而且通常非常明显。
Beta 环境极少使用，但当我们确实在进行长期实验时，就会把它放在那里。Staging 环境则用于短暂的部署前检查。
运行这些环境花费不菲，但能够看到运行 GPU 代码的结果让这一切物有所值。我们与 NVIDIA 的朋友们合作，让驱动程序和工具链正常工作，他们也曾作为企业赞助商支持了我们很长一段时间。感谢 NVIDIA！
显然，更好的信号是队列深度：即实际有多少编译任务在等待，而不是 CPU 看起来有多忙。我们已经针对部分环境编写了基于 ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible 的扩展策略，一旦基于队列的编译路径在各处承载了真实流量，我们就希望以此作为所有环境的扩展依据。
无论如何，几乎从不替换。偶尔会有一个实验性构建被替换，而每日构建顾名思义会自我替换：今天的 GCC 主干会悄悄取代昨天的。只有发布版本才会永远保留。
内容寻址至少让解决这个问题变得安全可靠：没有任何链接指向的镜像肯定是未使用的，因此清理工作可以自动化，而不需要我眯着眼睛看文件名并祈祷。那 111 个镜像中有很大一部分将是昨天的每日构建，它们已被今天的构建悄悄取代。
如果你询问 API，数字是 6,157，但这有点作弊：它将同一个 GCC 分别为 C、C++、Fortran 等各算了一次。按唯一名称算，是 4,291 个。去年 6 月，相应的数字是 4,724 和 81 种语言，所以我们仍然保持着相当不错的增长，而且这几乎全不是我做的：人们不断带着我从未听说过的语言和可用的 PR 出现。

通常，NFS 会在本地缓存数据，但它仍然会通过属性缓存向服务器验证缓存的元数据是否是最新的。即使文件数据已被缓存，你也要付出网络延迟的代价来检查它是否发生了变化。通过环回挂载的 SquashFS 镜像可以“洗去”NFS 的特性：squashfs 驱动看到的是一个本地块设备，而内核则完全不知道在这些缓存的块背后，是一个理论上可能会发生变化的 NFS 文件。对于不可变的编译器镜像来说，这是一个巨大的福音。
一个“作业”并不是一个编译器：有些构建一个东西，有些构建一整个家族。构建在 UTC 午夜开始并在我们的构建基础设施上排队，而另一个单独的工作流在早上 5:30 进行安装，这两者仍然互不知情，所以有时我们会安装昨天的构建。这已经在待办事项列表上了。
我们并没有完全犯傻：在运行每日构建之前，它会检查上游代码库在过去一周内是否有提交，如果没有任何变动，就会完全跳过构建。实验分支安静的一周几乎不会让我们产生什么成本。
如果你想了解血淋淋的细节，可以看 #6669。它最初发布时是 1500ms，然后有人尝试了 2 秒，接着被回退，十天后又改回了 2 秒。目前的默认值是 2000ms。
相比一年前的 0.00039 美元有所上涨，但这并不是因为什么东西变贵了。而是因为使用量下降了，而固定成本——所有的存储空间以及每晚构建所有编译器的开销——依然保持在原来的水平。
早在 2014 年我就做过同样的分析，基于总计近 200 万次编译，来研究是否可以淘汰 GCC 4.4。当时的默认编译器是 clang++ 3.0.6，占比 37%，所以即使其他一切都变了，列表的形态也没有太大变化。我没有淘汰 GCC 4.4，它现在依然存在。
这主要是我们的“编译器发现”步骤：在发布一个版本之前，我们会询问机器上的每个编译器它到底是什么以及它自称是什么，并将答案写入一个 JSON 文件，供网站读取。这仍然是一个手动步骤，偶尔会出错，不过我想我在最近的一次提交中已经让它稳定多了。我也在尝试使用 LLM “脚本”来帮助处理无法直接在代码中自动化的地方：有很多奇怪的边缘情况需要处理，把它们全部正确编码是很棘手的。
现代的 glibc 使用 SHT_RELR 重定位，这需要 binutils 2.38 或更高版本才能进行链接，而我们 29 个较旧的 GCC 自带了早于该版本的 ld。我们尝试从源码重新构建它们，结果引发了一连串的 libsanitizer 不兼容问题，所以我们放弃了，转而在安装时将这些编译器的 ld 软链接到一个较新的版本。后来 Partouf 正确地重新构建了其中几个。

blocks.text: Since LLMs have been available, I've been doing a lot of coding using agents. Unlike shoving AI into every app, replacing customer support with chatbots, generating endless streams of slop, etc., agentic coding is actually useful. If used right – and, crucially, by someone who understands and reviews the code before merging it – it's an incredible time saver.

In this post, I'm going to share some of the techniques that I've been using recently to get coding agents to 1) write high quality code that's easy to maintain, and 2) to do so securely, in such a way that the agent can't access data outside what it needs to achieve the task.
The AI industry sucks

But first, don't get me wrong. The AI industry is terrible. It's driving environmentally destructive data centers that everyone hates. It's consolidating power into the hands of a tiny group of reactionary billionaire weirdos that seem to genuinely believe they're building a god, and also that really want military contracts so they can build autonomous killing machines. It's flooding the internet with slop, and Google AI Overviews are spreading misinformation on an a scale unprecedented in human history.

The AI industry is a bubble built on hype and lies and debt, and the promise that executives can fire all their workers and still make lots of profit. It's a house of mirrors that will inevitably come crashing down. Anthropic and OpenAI sell $20/month plans knowing that if their users use as many tokens as they're given, it costs them way more money than it makes them. But they don't care because everything is fake. It's all terrible, and at some point soon, the whole thing will collapse.

I have no idea exactly what it will look like when that happens, but I do know that the era of cheap access to extremely powerful LLMs will end. It's only a matter of time before the actual costs will catch up to them. This already happened with GitHub Copilot. Starting in June, GitHub began charging based on actual usage, and it became way too expensive, so I (and many, many others) stopped using it.

Given this, I've decided that since agentic coding is able to write high quality code (if done correctly, not just by default lol) much faster than I can, and since frontier models are cheaper now than they ever will be again, I might as well take advantage of them while I can.
When everything crashes back down to earth, destroying the economy with it, hopefully we'll be left with some capable open models. And with our brains intact, too, of course.
Open weight models

When possible, I like using open weights models. I have a Framework Desktop server with 128GB of RAM and a GPU running an Ollama server, giving me access to private, local models. The best coding model I've found that runs on my hardware is qwen3-coder-next:q8_0 (84 GB), and the best vision model (that's able to look at images) that runs on my hardware is qwen3-vl:32b-thinking-q8_0 (35 GB).
But unfortunately, even qwen3-coder-next doesn't compare to the frontier models from Anthropic and OpenAI. Because of this, I use local LLMs for these purposes:

Code generation for secret projects, where I don't want to share any information about the project, like its source code, or the fact that it exists, with any third parties (like OpenAI, Anthropic, GitHub, etc.).

Direct data analysis with datasets that I don't want to share with third parties. (Though most of the time I'm writing code to help analyze data, the data might be sensitive, but the code itself isn't. In that case, I often use frontier models to write the code, and then I set the code loose on the private data.)

A local, private chatbot for simple tasks that don't require huge context windows or lots of reasoning. I use a local Open WebUI server to give me access to a chatbot interface in the style of ChatGPT or whatever, where I can manage multiple sessions.

I haven't really had a use for it, but I will totally use models if I need to do a large number of small repetitive tasks. For example, let's say I have a million screenshots, and I want to extract the URLs in browser windows from each screenshot (a saw talk last year where the researchers did this). I could do this with my local model for free, where I'd have to pay OpenAI or Anthropic for tokens to use their API.
Agentic coding tools

For awhile I was using Visual Studio Code and GitHub Copilot, but I stopped when I had to actually pay for my usage. It was just too expensive. I still use VS Code as an editor, but now I do agentic coding itself using CLI-based tools that differ depending on the model I'm using.
Here's what I use:
Claude Code CLI for Anthropic models like Opus 5 and Fable 5
Codex CLI for OpenAI models like GPT 5.6 Sol
OpenCode for my locally hosted models on Ollama
Both Claude and Codex have desktop apps, which I've tried. They're reasonably nice, but I prefer the CLI versions, especially because it makes it much easier to sandbox them.
LLM skills

The last few months, I've gotten really into using Matt Pockock's LLM skills. It's actually entirely changed the way I use LLMs for agentic coding. Here's a video where he explains his workflow, end-to-end:

I've found that using "grilling session," where the LLM relentlessly asks me a series of questions about the feature I'm making, and then uses the answers to write a spec, really helpful at uncovering and deciding on thorny implementation details before writing any code.

I've also found that allowing the LLM to interface with your issue tracker is kind of amazing, and allows you to use agents much more autonomously. The /to-tickets skill can help turn a detailed spec into a series of GitHub issues (or wherever you want to track your issues), and automatically label them things like "ready-for-agent" or "ready-for-human". The /implement skill can frequently implement an entire well-defined issue in one go, including doing a code review and creating a PR.

There are also some other skills that seem useful for certain codebases or tasks. I've been doing some mobile development using Expo, and I've found that Expo Skills are really good at doing thorny-but-tedious maintenance tasks like upgrading to a new version of Expo. And while I haven't tried these yet, I have my eye on this Trail of Bits repo of skills for security research.
Sandboxing the agents
Since I've been using the Matt Pocock skills, I've found that it's entirely feasible to tell codex something like:
$implement https://github.com/{link-to-an-issue}. Implement it in its own branch. When you're done, push your code and create a PR.
Then, 45 minutes later, you have a PR waiting for you to review. If the issue and test seams are well-defined, it's frequently even ready to merge as-is.

But to actually let the agent sit there doing its thing without constantly interrupting its work waiting for you to approve various access, you need to run it in the extremely unsafe YOLO mode, where you just say yes to everything.
With claude this is --dangerously-skip-permissions
With codex this is --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox
You obviously never should run agents like this directly on your computer. There are many options for sandboxing, but my current workflow is Docker Sandboxes, and it works great.
After you install Docker Sandboxes, you use the sbx  command to create and manage sandboxes and run agents (like Claude, Codex, OpenCode, etc.) inside a sandbox. Each sandbox is isolated so that:
It runs its own Docker VM for the sandbox container, so it doesn't share a Linux kernel with anything else.
The container is able to run other Docker containers within the same VM, so for example, if your tests rely on Docker Compose, it can still run your tests.

All network access is proxied through the host with a firewall of allowed domains. By default it only allows common coding domains for services like GitHub, NPM, PyPi, etc., but you can restrict it or open it up as much as you want, per-sandbox.
It supports credential isolation, so each sandbox can be configured different for authentication to OpenAI, Anthropic, GitHub, etc.
Isolating GitHub access

When the agent reads a GitHub issue, or opens a PR, or analyzes why an Actions workflow failed, it uses the GitHub CLI tool, gh , authenticated as you. The simplest way to authenticate to gh is just by logging in using a browser, basically giving gh full access to your GitHub account.

This might by fine for your personal gh use, but I wouldn't trust a coding agent with that access. If you're working on some fun hobby project, an agent that gets prompt injected could, for example, use gh to access all of your secret work repositories.
Instead, it's possible to create repo-scoped GitHub tokens, so that the agent is only allowed to go wild on the specific repo it's working on with limited permissions, and can't access anything else.
The actual mechanics of how I've set this up is pretty complicated, so I think I'll save it for a future post. But in short:

I create a GitHub fine-grained personal access token (PAT), strictly limiting it to the repo(s) that each specific sandbox will be working in. I store the PAT is the sbx secrets manager scoped just to that sandbox, which uses it to authenticate with gh inside the sandbox.

I create a dedicated SSH key (marked as signing-only in my GitHub account) for use by agents, for signing commits. I ensure my SSH agent forwards just this one signing key into the container, and no other SSH key.

Now, if an agent goes rogue, it will not only be contained in a Docker container, unable to wreak havoc on my computer, but it will also be contained to a single GitHub repo, unable to wreak havoc (or steal secrets from) unrelated projects.
I hope you found this helpful! Happy coding.
If you found this interesting, subscribe to get these posts emailed directly to your inbox. If you want to support my work, consider becoming a paid supporter.

translations: 自从 LLM 问世以来，我一直在大量使用智能体进行编程。与将 AI 塞进每个应用、用聊天机器人取代客服、生成源源不断的垃圾内容等做法不同，智能体编程确实很有用。如果使用得当——最关键的是，由在合并前理解并审查代码的人来使用——它能极大地节省时间。
在这篇文章中，我将分享我最近使用的一些技巧，让编程智能体能够 1) 编写易于维护的高质量代码，并且 2) 安全地执行此操作，确保智能体无法访问完成任务所需之外的数据。
AI 行业糟透了
但首先，别误会我的意思。AI 行业非常糟糕。它正在推动建设人人都讨厌的、破坏环境的数据中心。它正在将权力集中到一小撮反动的亿万富翁怪人手中，这些人似乎真的相信自己在造神，而且非常渴望获得军事合同，以便制造自动杀戮机器。它正在用垃圾内容淹没互联网，而 Google AI Overviews 正在以前所未有的规模传播错误信息。
AI 行业是一个建立在炒作、谎言和债务之上的泡沫，其承诺是高管们可以解雇所有员工并依然获取丰厚利润。这是一个镜花水月般的幻象，注定会崩塌。Anthropic 和 OpenAI 销售 20 美元/月的套餐，他们心里清楚，如果用户用尽分配给他们的 token，其成本将远超收益。但他们不在乎，因为一切都是虚假的。这一切都很糟糕，而且很快，整个行业就会崩溃。
我不知道当那一天到来时具体会是什么样子，但我确实知道，廉价使用极其强大的 LLM 的时代将会终结。实际成本追上他们只是时间问题。GitHub Copilot 已经发生了这种情况。从 6 月起，GitHub 开始根据实际使用量收费，变得过于昂贵，所以我（以及许许多多其他人）停止了使用。
鉴于此，我决定，既然智能体编程能够以比我快得多的速度编写高质量代码（前提是操作正确，而不是默认就行，哈哈），而且前沿模型现在的价格比未来任何时候都要便宜，我不如趁现在好好利用它们。
当一切跌回现实并摧毁经济时，希望我们还能留下一些强大的开源模型。当然，也希望我们的大脑还能完好无损。
开放权重模型

在可能的情况下，我喜欢使用开放权重模型。我有一台配备 128GB 内存和 GPU 的 Framework Desktop 服务器，运行着 Ollama 服务器，这让我能够使用私有的本地模型。我发现能在我的硬件上运行的最佳编程模型是 qwen3-coder-next:q8_0 (84 GB)，而能在我的硬件上运行的最佳视觉模型（能够查看图像）是 qwen3-vl:32b-thinking-q8_0 (35 GB)。
但遗憾的是，即使是 qwen3-coder-next 也无法与 Anthropic 和 OpenAI 的前沿模型相媲美。因此，我将本地 LLM 用于以下目的：
为机密项目生成代码，在这些项目中，我不想与任何第三方（如 OpenAI、Anthropic、GitHub 等）分享关于该项目的任何信息，比如其源代码，甚至该项目存在的事实。
直接分析我不愿与第三方共享的数据集。（虽然大多数时候我是在编写代码来辅助分析数据，数据可能比较敏感，但代码本身并不敏感。在这种情况下，我经常使用前沿模型来编写代码，然后让代码在私有数据上运行。）
一个用于简单任务的本地私有聊天机器人，这些任务不需要巨大的上下文窗口或大量推理。我使用本地的 Open WebUI 服务器来访问类似 ChatGPT 风格的聊天机器人界面，在这里我可以管理多个会话。
我目前还没真正用到它，但如果我需要执行大量小型的重复性任务，我绝对会使用模型。例如，假设我有一百万张截图，我想从每张截图的浏览器窗口中提取 URL（我去年看了一个研究人员做这件事的演讲）。我可以用我的本地模型免费完成这个任务，而使用 OpenAI 或 Anthropic 的 API 则需要支付 token 费用。
智能体编程工具
有一段时间我使用 Visual Studio Code 和 GitHub Copilot，但当我必须为使用量付费时我就停用了。那太贵了。我仍然使用 VS Code 作为编辑器，但现在我使用基于 CLI 的工具来进行智能体编程，具体工具取决于我使用的模型。
这是我使用的工具：
用于 Anthropic 模型（如 Opus 5 和 Fable 5）的 Claude Code CLI
用于 OpenAI 模型（如 GPT 5.6 Sol）的 Codex CLI
用于我在 Ollama 上本地托管的模型的 OpenCode
Claude 和 Codex 都有桌面应用程序，我都试过。它们相当不错，但我更喜欢 CLI 版本，特别是因为它让沙盒化变得容易得多。
LLM 技能
过去几个月，我非常沉迷于使用 Matt Pockock 的 LLM 技能。它实际上完全改变了我使用 LLM 进行智能体编程的方式。这是一个他端到端解释其工作流的视频：
我发现使用“盘问会话”（grilling session）非常有帮助，在这个过程中，LLM 会不断向我提出一系列关于我正在开发的功能的问题，然后利用这些答案编写规范，这有助于在编写任何代码之前发现并确定棘手的实现细节。

我还发现，让 LLM 与你的问题追踪系统对接非常棒，这能让你更加自主地使用智能体。/to-tickets 技能可以帮助将详细的规范转化为一系列 GitHub issue（或者任何你想追踪问题的地方），并自动给它们打上诸如 "ready-for-agent" 或 "ready-for-human" 的标签。/implement 技能通常可以一次性实现一个定义明确的 issue，包括进行代码审查和创建 PR。
还有一些其他技能似乎对某些代码库或任务很有用。我一直在使用 Expo 进行一些移动开发，我发现 Expo Skills 非常擅长处理棘手但繁琐的维护任务，比如升级到新版本的 Expo。虽然我还没试过，但我正关注着这个用于安全研究的 Trail of Bits 技能库。
沙盒化智能体
自从我开始使用 Matt Pocock 的技能以来，我发现完全可以这样告诉 codex：
$implement https://github.com/{link-to-an-issue}. 在它自己的分支中实现它。完成后，推送你的代码并创建一个 PR。
然后，45 分钟后，你就有了一个等待你审查的 PR。如果 issue 和测试切入点定义明确，它通常甚至可以直接按原样合并。
但要想让 agent 真正坐在那里执行任务，而不是不断打断工作等待你批准各种访问权限，你需要在极不安全的 YOLO 模式下运行它，也就是对所有操作都直接放行。
对于 claude，这个参数是 --dangerously-skip-permissions
对于 codex，这个参数是 --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox
显然，你绝不应该直接在自己的电脑上这样运行 agent。沙盒化的方案有很多，但我目前的工作流是使用 Docker Sandboxes，效果非常好。
安装 Docker Sandboxes 后，你可以使用 sbx 命令来创建和管理沙盒，并在沙盒内运行 agent（如 Claude、Codex、OpenCode 等）。每个沙盒都是隔离的，因此：
它为沙盒容器运行自己的 Docker 虚拟机，因此不会与其他任何东西共享 Linux 内核。
该容器能够在同一个虚拟机内运行其他 Docker 容器，例如，如果你的测试依赖 Docker Compose，它依然可以正常运行测试。
所有网络访问都通过主机代理，并配有允许访问的域名防火墙。默认情况下，它只允许访问 GitHub、NPM、PyPi 等服务的常见编程域名，但你可以根据需要针对每个沙盒进行限制或开放。
它支持凭据隔离，因此每个沙盒都可以针对 OpenAI、Anthropic、GitHub 等配置不同的身份验证方式。
隔离 GitHub 访问权限
当 agent 读取 GitHub issue、提交 PR 或分析 Actions 工作流失败的原因时，它会使用 GitHub CLI 工具 gh，并以你的身份进行验证。验证 gh 最简单的方法就是使用浏览器登录，这基本上等于赋予了 gh 对你 GitHub 账户的完全访问权限。
这对于你个人使用 gh 可能没问题，但我不会放心让编程 agent 拥有这种权限。如果你正在开发某个有趣的业余项目，一个遭到提示词注入的 agent 可能会利用 gh 访问你所有机密的工作仓库。
相反，我们可以创建限定仓库范围的 GitHub token，这样 agent 就只能在它正在处理的特定仓库内以受限权限进行操作，而无法访问其他任何内容。
我设置这套机制的具体操作相当复杂，所以我打算留到以后的文章中再讲。简而言之：
我创建了一个 GitHub 细粒度个人访问令牌（PAT），严格将其限制在每个特定沙盒将要处理的仓库范围内。我将该 PAT 存储在仅限该沙盒作用域的 sbx 密钥管理器中，沙盒内的 gh 会使用它进行身份验证。
我创建了一个专用的 SSH 密钥（在我的 GitHub 账户中标记为仅用于签名）供 agent 使用，以对提交进行签名。我确保我的 SSH agent 只将这一个签名密钥转发到容器中，而不转发任何其他 SSH 密钥。
现在，如果某个 agent 失控，它不仅会被限制在 Docker 容器中，无法对我的电脑造成破坏，而且还会被限制在单个 GitHub 仓库内，无法对无关项目造成破坏（或窃取机密）。
希望这些内容对你有帮助！祝你编程愉快。
如果你觉得这些内容有趣，请订阅以将这些文章直接发送到你的收件箱。如果你想支持我的工作，可以考虑成为付费支持者。
